title: TA7-09016
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of Haïti, and her minor son, XXXXX XXXXX, a citizen of the United States of America (USA), claim refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). XXXXX XXXXX was designated as the representative of her son for the purposes of his claim. Their claims have been heard jointly pursuant to Rule 49 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.2 ALLEGATIONS
The principal claimant alleges the following:

She fled Haïti in XXXXX 1994, a day after the murder of her mother, brother and sister. The principal claimant was a XXXXX XXXXX and had a XXXXX XXXXX in Port-au-Prince since 1989. She was a supporter of Aristide and a member of his organization. After the military coup d'état of September 1991, anti-Lavalas men looted and destroyed her XXXXX. The principal claimant fled to XXXXX XXXXX In XXXXX 1994, feeling safer, the principal claimant returned to Port-au-Prince and reopened a XXXXX XXXXX On XXXXX, 1994, two soldiers and two unknown men followed the principal claimant home, entered and killed her mother, brother and sister. The principal claimant had not noticed that they had entered until she heard the commotion in another room. She was able to see the assailants and the victims and she fled through the back of the house. The next day she left Haïti for the USA. Her claim for asylum was denied in the USA. The principal claimant says that she was not told why. She came to Canada on XXXXX XXXXX 2007 and filed a claim.
The principal claimant fears being persecuted by anti-Lavalas people by reason of her political opinions if she returns to Haïti and because of what she witnessed.
The panel finds that the claimants are not refugees or persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Guidelines
The panel has given consideration to the Chairperson's guidelines on gender-related persecution.3 Identity
The principal claimant's oral testimony and the documentation filed establish her Haïtian nationality and the nationality of her son as a USA citizen.4 Credibility
The principal claimant's testimony was precise, consistent and credible. Well-Foundedness

The principal claimant testified that she did not know why the members of her family had been killed. Although she had been aware of the presence of men behind her, she had not realized that they were following her and that they had entered the house. She went directly to another room. It is when she heard shots and screams that she realized what was happening. She saw the scene through an opening and she fled by the back. She said that times were particularly bad in 1994 and, although this was the first time to her knowledge she was followed, this type of incident happened all the time in the neighbourhood. She fears being persecuted today by the same men who killed members of her family, whom she calls "attachés", and by other anti-Lavalas people because she helped the cause of Aristide at one time. She says her sister told her in recent years that people were enquiring about her from time to time and that, in XXXXX 2009, masked men went to the house where her children live, tied them up and asked for USA money.

Although she speculates that the assailant may have been after her, the principal claimant admits that she does not know if this was the case or why the murders were committed. Tragic as it was, the panel finds that the evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the murder of the principal claimant's mother and siblings was for reasons of the principal claimant's political opinions or for any other reason mentioned in section 96 of the IRPA. Furthermore, the courts have established that witnessing a murder does not by itself create a nexus to section 96 of the IRPA.5

As for the looting and destruction of the principal claimant's XXXXX three years earlier, in 1991, by anti-Lavalas people, the panel finds that, on the balance of probabilities, it appears to have been for the reason of the principal claimant's real or perceived political opinion and her previous political involvement. However, the panel finds that such destruction of property does not amount to persecution pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA. Persecution is not defined in the IRPA. It has fallen to the courts to identify the boundaries of the word. First, to be considered persecution, the mistreatment must be serious.6 The courts have equated the notion with a key denial of core human rights.7 "...the essential question is whether the persecution alleged by the claimant threatens his or her basic human rights in a fundamental way."8

A second criterion is that the inflicting of harm occurs with repetition or persistence, or in a systematic way.9 The principal claimant has described a single such incident. The panel finds that this does not constitute a "key denial of core human rights". On the basis of the evidence, the panel finds that the principal claimant has not demonstrated that, on the balance of probabilities, she had suffered persecution.

However, refugee protection is forward looking and the panel must assess what the principal claimant fears today and in the future, in Haïti. Her testimony was clear in this regard; she fears being persecuted by anti-Lavalas people by reason of her political opinions, and by those who killed her mother and siblings. While the principal claimant did not invoke this as such in her testimony, her counsel has argued that the principal claimant would also be at risk of rape in Haïti and at risk of kidnapping and extortion because she would be known to have lived in the USA and assumed to have money.

Fifteen years have elapsed since the horrible events recounted by the principal claimant, more since her limited political involvement. The principal claimant was not in anyway a significant political figure. The documentary evidence reveals that while political violence may not have totally disappeared in Haïti, it has much abated and no longer represents a serious threat. "...the situation has calmed down...Today, freedom of expression is tolerated much more, but people are still cautious...."10 "Multiparty presidential and parliamentary elections in February and March 2006 were relatively stable and peaceful."11 "In Port-au-Prince "...gang capacity to carry out political violence, kidnapping, port blockades and business sector coercion on a large scale has been eviscerated."12 "Levels of politically motivated violence remained low, but high rates of unemployment, widespread poverty and drug trafficking resulted in social unrest and violence."13 " ...in Haïti, political violence has transformed into violence from organized crime..."14

The evidence does not show that, on the balance of probabilities, the principal claimant would be deemed to be a threat to the ruling party or to any other party in Haïti, or to be in anyway a significant political figure, nor does the evidence demonstrate a serious possibility that the principal claimant would face persecution for reasons of real or perceived political opinion upon returning to Haïti. The panel finds that the principal claimant's alleged fear in this regard constitutes speculation and is not well-founded, and that the principal claimant has failed to establish a nexus with any of the reasons mentioned in section 96 of the IRPA.

There remains the question of whether the principal claimant's removal to Haïti would, on the balance of probabilities, subject her personally to a danger of torture, or to a risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. As stated, fifteen years have elapsed since the last tragic events recounted by the principal claimant. The principal claimant stated that such events were not unusual during those difficult times. She does not know that the men were after her. They do not know that she has seen them. The panel finds that the evidence does not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant would be exposed personally to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, upon returning to Haïti today. The panel finds that the harm that the principal claimant fears is of the nature of criminal acts. The Federal Court has stated in Prophète15, that "...the risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haïtians..."16. Gender

While the principal claimant did not expressly invoke the issue of gender and rape as such, her counsel argued that by reason of her gender the principal claimant would be at risk in Haïti. The documentation filed in evidence demonstrates that violence against women is unfortunately a reality in Haïti and that protection is inadequate: "Women and girls continued to face widespread discrimination and violence in all aspects of public and private life..." 17. "Rape is "commonplace" in Haïti. The number has increased in 2008. It is often left unpunished and is treated in practice as a "relatively minor infraction".18
However, such violence is not isolated and the documentary evidence shows that criminality of all sorts is rampant in Haïti.19

In Ward20, which referred among other things to the grounds of membership in a particular social group, the Supreme Court of Canada defined such a group as, amongst others, "groups defined by an innate or unchangeable characteristic..." and described gender as an example of such a group.

However, In Soimin21, the Federal Court upheld a negative Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision concerning a Haïtian woman whose claim was based in part on a fear of persecution in the form of rape. The Federal Court upheld the Member's finding that the root or source of the claimant's fear was generalized crime rather than her membership in a particular social group: " The violence feared by the applicant arises from general criminal activity in Haïti, and not the discriminatory targeting of women in particular. The harm feared is criminal in nature and has no nexus to the Convention refugee definition...The risk alleged by the applicant is a random risk shared by everyone who lives in her country;"22

More recently, in Lozandier23, concerning a Haïtian woman whose claimed was also partly based on the fear of rape, the Federal Court reiterated that the source of the claimant's fear was generalized crime rather than her gender: "En somme, le risqué que la demanderesse allègue est un risque aléatoire auquel font face indistinctement de façon générale toutes les personnes vivant dans son pays..."24

Therefore, the panel finds that the fear alleged by the principal claimant is based on general criminality and is not for reason of her membership in a particular social group nor for reason of any other ground mentioned in section 96 of the IRPA. Thus, the panel finds that the fear based on her gender is not well-founded. Diaspora

The principal claimant's counsel has also argued that the principal claimant could be a target for extortion because she would be perceived as wealthy as evidenced by the attack on her children and the demand for money.

The Federal Court concluded in Cius25 that Diaspora returnees do not constitute a particular social group; the perception of wealth is insufficient to this effect. " ... The perception of wealth is insufficient to sustain the position that Haïtian returnees constitute a social group."26 " ... people returning to Haïti after a stay abroad do not constitute a particular social group within the meaning of section 96 of the Act."27

Furthermore, as to the question whether the perception of wealth gives rise to a danger pursuant to section 97 of IRPA, the Federal Court also concluded in Cius that such a risk is generalized and not personal to the claimant. " ... the risk faced by the applicant is generalized. The risk of violence is one which every person in Haïti faces."28

The Federal Court confirmed in Prophète that such a risk is a generalized risk faced by all the citizens of Haïti. "Based on the recent jurisprudence of his Court, I am of the view that the applicant does not face a personalized risk that is not faced generally by other individuals in or from Haïti. The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haïtians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haïtians are at risk of becoming the victims of violence."29

For all of the above reasons, the panel finds that the principal claimant is not a member of a particular social group pursuant to section 96 of IRPA and is not a person entitled to protection pursuant to section 97 of IRPA.
With respect to the claimant XXXXX XXXXX, who is USA born, no evidence of any nature was presented in support of his claim.

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel finds that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, and rejects their claims.
